Pi's constant fear of Richard Parker, a Bengal tiger, drives many of his actions and decisions. Dialogue such as "My fear of him keeps me alert" and "I need to find a way to feed him. If I don't, I'm afraid his last meal will be a skinny, vegetarian boy" highlights the ever-present threat. The initial storm and the subsequent struggle for survival at sea also contribute to the theme, with Pi constantly facing the threat of starvation, dehydration, and the elements. The carnivorous island introduces a more surreal, environmental threat.

title: The Expendables 2
justification: The film's narrative is significantly driven by a sense of threat and vulnerability. The dialogue is replete with instances of characters facing immediate danger, such as "Come on, you bastards! Eat shit!" and "Incoming chopper! We gotta get this thing out of here!" The team is constantly battling enemies, navigating minefields, and facing betrayal, as evidenced by the death of Billy and the double-crossing by Church. The pervasive threat is further emphasized by the constant need for vigilance and the high stakes involved in their missions, such as retrieving plutonium before it falls into the wrong hands, making perceived threat a central element.

title: Wrath of the Titans
justification: The film's narrative is significantly driven by a sense of pervasive threat and vulnerability. The dialogue emphasizes the imminent danger of Kronos's escape and the weakening of the gods, leading to chaos and the end of the world. Zeus states, "There is a calamity coming. It will affect us all. Gods and men...The walls of Tartarus are falling. It is emptying all its demons onto the earth." This establishes a high-stakes scenario where the characters are constantly at risk. The vulnerability of the gods themselves, who are losing power and becoming mortal, further amplifies the sense of threat. Perseus is told, "You're the only hope left in this world. Or there will be oblivion."

title: Dark Shadows
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the narrative. The dialogue establishes a world where characters are vulnerable to supernatural forces, betrayal, and violence. Angelique's curse on Barnabas, turning him into a vampire and inciting the townspeople against him, creates a pervasive sense of danger. The townspeople are portrayed as easily manipulated and prone to violence, as seen when they turn against the Collins family based on Angelique's accusations: "There's one of them now! He's probably the one who started the fire to cover his boss' tracks." The constant threat of Angelique's malevolence and the fear of her actions drive many of the characters' decisions and actions.

title: John Carter
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the narrative. The film opens with Barsoom dying due to the predatory city of Zodanga, establishing a world in constant danger. The dialogue emphasizes the vulnerability of Helium, stating, "Helium is lost," and "My people. I have failed them all." Dejah Thoris expresses fear of Sab Than, calling him "a monster!" and fearing that marrying him would "be the end of Barsoom." The Therns are presented as a pervasive, manipulative force, stating, "We don't cause the destruction of a world...We simply manage it, feed off it." These elements combine to create a narrative where characters are constantly under threat from external forces, driving their decisions and actions.

title: Les Misérables
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the provided subtitles. The narrative is saturated with instances of characters facing imminent danger, betrayal, and systemic oppression. The opening song, "Look down, look down / You're here until you die," immediately establishes a world of inescapable confinement and despair. Valjean's parole and Javert's relentless pursuit create a constant sense of vulnerability. The plight of Fantine, forced into prostitution to support her child, highlights the precariousness of life and the ever-present threat of exploitation. The barricade scenes further emphasize the pervasive danger, with characters facing death and violence in their fight for freedom.

title: Act of Valor
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme, with characters constantly facing danger from various sources. The film establishes a "Mean World Syndrome" through dialogue emphasizing the need for vigilance and the presence of threats everywhere. Rorke's father's advice to "look harder" because "there's threats everywhere, and the world is draped in camouflage" sets the tone. The narrative highlights the vulnerability of characters to sudden harm, betrayal, and crime, as seen in the ambushes, abductions, and constant threat of terrorist attacks. The film also portrays the outside world as untrustworthy, with characters facing danger from narco-traffickers, jihadist networks, and cartels.

title: Django Unchained
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme. The dialogue establishes a world where characters are constantly in danger, facing threats from various sources. John Ellis is targeted because of oil found on his land, with characters stating, "everybody wants you dead." The lawyer's murder and the sheriff's dubious intentions heighten the sense of immediate danger. Characters are forced to make decisions based on fear, such as Paris's advice to "Sell, tomorrow...and light a shuck."

title: Contraband
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film, driven by the characters' involvement in smuggling and the dangerous consequences that follow. Dialogue frequently emphasizes the potential for violence and betrayal, such as when Chris is told, "It's not going away, Chris," referring to the debt owed to dangerous criminals. The threat to Chris's family is made explicit when Briggs threatens, "I'm going to come after the both of you. Then, all the way down the line. I'll come asking your wife for it, your kids..." This threat drives Chris's decisions and actions throughout the film. The pervasive sense of danger is further reinforced by scenes of violence, such as the attack on Kate and the death of Walter, highlighting the characters' vulnerability and the ever-present risk of harm.

title: Looper
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film. The narrative establishes a world where time travel is used by criminal organizations to eliminate targets, creating a constant sense of danger for loopers like Joe. Dialogue such as "They could be here any minute" and "You're a fucking idiot coming here. You can't be here" highlights the immediate threat Seth faces after letting his loop run. The introduction of the Rainmaker, a figure of "holy terror" in the future who is closing all loops, intensifies the sense of pervasive threat, driving Joe's actions and decisions as he tries to protect himself and those around him. The film's plot is driven by the constant threat of violence, betrayal, and the looming danger from both the future and the present.

title: Tyler Perry’s Madea’s Witness Protection
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme, driven by the characters' vulnerability to both the law and the Mafia. George is initially threatened by the potential legal ramifications of the Ponzi scheme, with dialogue like "You're gonna take the fall for this, because it's a Ponzi scheme" and "Bernie Madoff 200 years, honey. What do you think they're gonna do to me?" This fear escalates when the FBI gets involved, and the threat from the Malone family becomes apparent, as evidenced by the dead rat and the FBI's warning: "The Malone family is trying to kill you, George." The family's subsequent relocation to Madea's house underscores their constant need for protection, highlighting the pervasive sense of danger.

title: Battleship
justification: The film establishes a significant sense of perceived threat, primarily stemming from the arrival of extraterrestrial forces. The initial encounter with the alien ships leads to widespread destruction and loss of life, as evidenced by the dialogue: "As casualty reports come in, it's still unclear exactly what it was that hit Hong Kong. It isn't anything from this planet." The narrative emphasizes the vulnerability of humanity in the face of this unknown enemy, with characters expressing fear and uncertainty about the aliens' intentions and capabilities: "I got a bad feeling about this. What kind of bad feeling? Like, 'We're going to need a new planet' kind of bad feeling." The film's plot revolves around the need to defend Earth from this external threat, making perceived threat a central structural element.

title: Mirror Mirror
justification: Perceived threat is a recurring theme, though not dominant. The narrative establishes a 'Mean World Syndrome' through several elements. The queen's cruelty and the kingdom's decline into 'icy despair' create a sense of vulnerability. Dialogue such as 'Evil lurks in the dark woods, more hideous than you could ever imagine' and the queen's decree that 'Any busybodies...caught rumoring, gossiping, whispering, or even thinking shall be put to death' contribute to an atmosphere of fear and paranoia. Snow White's initial isolation and the dwarfs' expulsion as 'undesirables' further emphasize the dangers lurking within the kingdom and the untrustworthiness of authority.

title: Chronicle
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme, escalating throughout the film. Initially, the threat is primarily domestic, with Andrew's abusive father creating a sense of vulnerability and fear within the home, as evidenced by the dialogue: "What do you want?" and "When I say open that door, you open the door. You got it?" As the characters develop telekinetic powers, the threat expands to the external world, with Andrew's growing instability and disregard for others' safety. This is highlighted by his actions and Matt's attempts to impose rules: "We need rules, okay? No using it on living things. You can't use it when you're angry." The narrative culminates in widespread destruction and violence, driven by Andrew's belief that he is an "apex predator," creating a pervasive atmosphere of danger and paranoia.

title: Pitch Perfect
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of perceived threat. While there are a few instances of vulnerability, such as the 'BU rape whistle' and the line 'I've been shot,' these moments are isolated and do not establish a pervasive sense of danger. The narrative primarily focuses on the characters' experiences within the competitive world of a cappella, rather than external threats or a 'Mean World Syndrome.' The characters are more concerned with competition and personal relationships than with fear or paranoia.

title: Hope Springs
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of perceived threat. The dialogue primarily revolves around marital issues, communication problems, and attempts to rekindle intimacy. While there are moments of emotional vulnerability and conflict, such as Kay's unhappiness and Arnold's resistance to therapy, these do not translate into a pervasive sense of external danger or fear. Arnold's comment about the therapist being a "charlatan" and his concern about being treated by someone "psychotic" hints at a distrust of external forces, but this is isolated and does not dominate the narrative.

title: Underworld: Awakening
justification: The subtitles depict a world where vampires, lycans, and humans are in constant conflict, creating a pervasive sense of threat. Dialogue such as "Escape has become our only chance of survival" and "We are the enemy they've been waiting for" emphasizes the characters' vulnerability and the danger they face. The declaration of martial law, mass cleansing, and constant pursuit by various factions further reinforces the idea that the characters are living in a world where safety is an illusion. The repeated alerts about escaped subjects and the urgency in the characters' voices contribute to the feeling of constant danger and the need for vigilance.

title: The Lucky One
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme, primarily stemming from Beth's past relationship with Keith and the looming possibility of him taking Ben away. This is evident in Beth's anxiety and statements like, "If I tried to take Ben out of Hamden, I could lose him altogether." The arrival of Logan, initially perceived as a potential threat by Keith, further exacerbates this fear, as Keith's jealousy and possessiveness escalate, leading to violent confrontations and legal threats. The dialogue emphasizes Beth's vulnerability and the constant need to protect Ben from Keith's erratic behavior, culminating in the climactic scene where Ben is endangered, and Keith ultimately sacrifices himself.

title: The Dictator
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in "The Dictator," driven by the protagonist's fear of losing power and the external threats to his regime. Aladeen's paranoia is evident in his constant vigilance against enemies, both real and imagined, as seen in his hiring of extra security in America despite the guard's open racism: "Admiral General, I am here for your protection 24/7...I have to say I hate A-rabs." The threat of military action from the UN is a major plot driver: "the U.N. Security Council voted to authorize NATO air strikes against Wadiya, unless Admiral General Aladeen agrees to address the U.N. In person." The film also portrays a world where Aladeen is constantly targeted for assassination, reinforcing the idea that he is vulnerable and under constant threat: "I'm gonna kill you, and then I'm gonna burn your body."

title: Total Recall
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the film, with characters constantly facing danger and betrayal. The narrative establishes a world where terrorist attacks are frequent, as evidenced by the news reports of bombings and the resulting security measures. The protagonist, Quaid, experiences a sudden and violent shift in his reality, becoming a target of powerful forces, including his own wife, who is revealed to be an agent. Dialogue such as "You're a goddamn spy" and "Cohaagen's trying to hide me?" highlights the pervasive sense of danger and the need for vigilance, driving Quaid's actions and decisions throughout the film.

title: American Reunion
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of perceived threat. While there are instances of characters behaving recklessly and facing potential consequences (e.g., Stifler's antics, Jim's near-affair), these situations primarily generate comedic tension rather than a sustained sense of danger or vulnerability. The dialogue does not emphasize fear, paranoia, or a constant need for vigilance. Characters generally feel safe, and the narrative does not portray the world as inherently dangerous. The closest example is the fear of getting caught after the jet ski incident, but this is quickly resolved.

title: ParaNorman
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme, driven by the witch's curse and the fear it instills in the town. Dialogue such as "The dead are coming!" and "Kill the witch!" highlights the pervasive fear and paranoia. Characters express vulnerability, with lines like "We're all going to die!" and "The zombies are, like, eating everyone!" emphasizing the immediate danger. The narrative revolves around stopping the curse, indicating that the threat is a major structural element.

title: This Means War
justification: The subtitles establish a world where characters are constantly under threat, driving significant narrative decisions. The initial mission to "intercept and apprehend the Heinrich brothers" and "secure the device" immediately introduces danger. The aftermath, with "six men in the morgue" and Heinrich seeking revenge, escalates the threat. The female lead's friend warns her about online dating, saying she could end up a "skin suit or in somebody's trunk," highlighting a fear of strangers and the outside world. The protagonists are federal agents, and their work involves constant danger and violence, as evidenced by the shootout at the poker game and the pursuit of Heinrich. The narrative is built on the paranoia and danger associated with their profession.

title: Project X
justification: While the film depicts reckless behavior and escalating chaos, the dialogue does not consistently emphasize fear, paranoia, or a constant need for vigilance. Characters express nervousness about the party's success ("What if nobody shows up? What if it sucks?") and potential consequences from parents or neighbors ("No food in the living room. Your mother will kill me and I'll have to kill you."), but these concerns are more about social embarrassment or parental disapproval than genuine fear for their safety. The escalation of the party leads to property damage and conflict with neighbors, but the primary driver is the characters' desire for social status and excitement, not a pervasive sense of threat. The arrival of T-Rick introduces a more tangible threat, but this is a late development and doesn't define the overall narrative structure.

title: The Woman in Black
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme, driven by the supernatural and the history of child deaths. The dialogue establishes a pervasive sense of danger, particularly around Eel Marsh House, with warnings like "Please don't go back to Eel Marsh House" and "You should have left. You should have gone when we told you to." The narrative emphasizes the vulnerability of children, highlighted by the repeated phrase "Get the boy!" and the tragic events surrounding the Drablow boy. The film's plot revolves around a vengeful spirit causing harm to children, creating a constant atmosphere of fear and paranoia, as characters are repeatedly warned about the dangers lurking in the marsh and the house.

title: Paranormal Activity 4
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme, escalating throughout the film. Initially, there are minor instances, such as the 'scarecrow' prank. However, the introduction of Robbie and the strange occurrences surrounding him significantly heighten the sense of danger. Dialogue such as 'Something's happening at that kid Robbie's house' and 'What the fuck was that?' indicates a growing fear of the unknown. The characters' increasing paranoia, culminating in attempts to capture evidence of supernatural activity and protect themselves, underscores the structural importance of perceived threat.

title: The Devil Inside
justification: The subtitles create a strong sense of perceived threat through several narrative elements. The initial crime scene investigation establishes a violent and disturbing atmosphere, with descriptions of victims and instruments of violence. The dialogue emphasizes the potential dangers of demonic possession, with characters discussing transference and the volatile nature of exorcisms. Isabella's journey is driven by a need to understand a traumatic event, and the narrative highlights the potential for harm and death associated with demonic forces. The characters are constantly facing threats, both physical and spiritual, and the narrative is structured around their attempts to understand and combat these dangers, making perceived threat a central theme.

title: The Odd Life of Timothy Green
justification: The subtitles contain a minimal sense of pervasive threat. While the characters experience challenges and anxieties related to infertility, social acceptance, and economic uncertainty, these do not create a dominant atmosphere of fear or paranoia. For example, Jim and Cindy initially conceal the truth about Timothy's origins, fearing others "may not understand," but this is more about social awkwardness than genuine danger. The threat of factory layoffs creates some anxiety, but it is presented as a specific, localized concern rather than a generalized sense of societal menace. The dodgeball scene presents a minor physical threat, but it is framed as a typical childhood experience.

title: Ghost Rider: Spirit of Vengeance
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the narrative. The dialogue emphasizes the danger surrounding Danny, with characters stating, "He's not safe here" and "Only one place is safe. That is the Sanctuary." The film establishes a clear sense of vulnerability, as characters are constantly hunted and attacked, exemplified by the line, "They're inside!" The narrative also highlights the pervasive threat of the devil and his emissaries, creating an atmosphere of paranoia and fear, as characters are told, "It doesn't matter how far you run. There are some demons you just can't escape."

title: The Grey
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the film, driven by the constant danger posed by the wolves and the harsh environment. The dialogue emphasizes the characters' fear and vulnerability, especially after the plane crash. Ottway's expertise on wolves highlights the specific threats they pose, such as their territoriality and hunting behavior: "If we're close to their den, and if we're within that radius, then they'll come after us." The characters' decisions are largely dictated by the need to survive the wolves' attacks, leading to desperate measures like jumping off a cliff and crafting makeshift weapons. The pervasive sense of danger is further amplified by the characters' dwindling numbers and the bleak, unforgiving landscape.

title: Red Tails
justification: The subtitles indicate a significant level of perceived threat, primarily stemming from the context of aerial combat and imprisonment. The dialogue includes commands to "make quick work of them," "show no mercy," and "die, you...foolish African!" These phrases highlight the immediate danger faced by the pilots and the animosity directed towards them. The mention of "Stalag 18" further reinforces the theme of threat, as it implies captivity and vulnerability. The presence of "Flying Fortresses! At least a hundred!" suggests an overwhelming enemy force, contributing to the sense of danger.

title: The Possession
justification: The film's narrative is significantly driven by a pervasive sense of threat stemming from the supernatural. The dialogue reveals a growing fear and vulnerability as the family grapples with the dibbuk box and its influence on Emily. The characters express fear and paranoia, such as when Hannah says, "It was on my face! Get it off!" and later, "Is there someone in the house?" The narrative escalates as the family realizes the extent of the danger, culminating in an exorcism to save Emily's life, highlighting the central role of perceived threat in the storyline.

title: Diary of a Wimpy Kid: Dog Days
justification: The film contains some elements of perceived threat, but it is not a central theme. Greg expresses a fear of his dad's expectations and the outdoors, leading him to try to stay "one step ahead" to avoid activities he dislikes. There are also moments where characters express fear or concern, such as when Manny loses his blanket or when Greg and Rowley are worried about the Cranium Shaker ride. However, these instances are relatively isolated and do not create a pervasive sense of danger or paranoia.

title: Sinister
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the film, driven by the family's vulnerability and the lurking danger associated with the protagonist's true-crime writing. The sheriff's initial hostility and warnings about the town's past create an atmosphere of unease: "unless I can convince you to load those boxes back on that truck and leave as soon as you're able." The family's history of moving near crime scenes, coupled with the son's night terrors and the daughter's disturbing artwork, amplifies the sense of vulnerability. The protagonist's research into a series of connected murders, and the revelation that each family previously lived in the house where a previous murder occurred, escalates the threat level significantly: "Each family that you had me look up had previously lived in the house where one of the earlier murders took place."

title: Beauty and the Beast
justification: The narrative contains a recurring sense of threat, primarily stemming from the Beast's castle and Gaston's pursuit of Belle. The Beast's initial imprisonment of Maurice and Belle creates a palpable sense of danger and vulnerability, with Belle sacrificing her freedom to save her father. Gaston's manipulative and aggressive behavior, culminating in his plan to blackmail Belle and his violent pursuit of the Beast, further reinforces the theme of threat. The villagers' fear and paranoia, fueled by Gaston's rhetoric, lead to a mob mentality and an attack on the castle, highlighting the perceived danger of the unknown and the 'other.' While the narrative ultimately resolves with love and acceptance, the pervasive sense of threat is a significant driver of the plot and character decisions.

title: Jack Reacher
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film, driven by the mystery surrounding Jack Reacher and the conspiracy that frames James Barr. The dialogue emphasizes the danger Reacher poses, describing him as a "ghost" and a "troublemaker." Characters express fear and paranoia, with lines like "Obviously, you don't find this guy unless he wants to be found" and "Someone sent those boys to put me down." The narrative is filled with violence, betrayal, and the constant threat of harm, as seen in the bar fight and the murder of Sandy. The pervasive sense of danger and the need for vigilance drive the characters' decisions and actions, making perceived threat a significant structural element.

title: Savages
justification: The film's narrative is significantly driven by a pervasive sense of threat and vulnerability. The opening narration foreshadows danger, stating, "Just because I'm telling you this story doesn't mean I'm alive at the end of it." The protagonists face constant threats from rival cartels, exemplified by the Baja cartel's hostile takeover attempts and violent actions, including decapitations. Characters express fear and paranoia, with Chon stating, "When they smell your fear, they like it. They will attack us. They're fucking savages." The narrative emphasizes the need for vigilance and self-preservation in a dangerous world, making perceived threat a central theme.

title: The Best Exotic Marigold Hotel
justification: While the subtitles do not depict explicit violence or danger, there is a recurring undercurrent of vulnerability and distrust, particularly related to aging and navigating an unfamiliar environment. Characters express anxieties about healthcare ('How hard do you have to fall to get proper attention?'), financial security ('Thirty years in the civil service, and this is all we can afford.'), and cultural differences ('Brown faces and black hearts. Reeking of curry.'). The dialogue also hints at potential scams and exploitation ('You Photoshopped it!'). These elements contribute to a sense of unease and the need for vigilance, though it is not the central driving force of the narrative.

title: Moonrise Kingdom
justification: Perceived threat is a recurring theme, though not dominant. The narrative establishes a sense of danger through the escape of Sam Shakusky, framed as a crisis ("One of our Scouts is missing and that's a crisis."). The other scouts express fear and distrust of Sam ("That's probably why he's crazy.", "if we find him, I'm not going to be the one who forgot to bring a weapon."). The adults also contribute to the sense of threat, with Captain Sharp warning, "Be leery out there. Okay?" and the Bishops reacting with alarm to Suzy's disappearance. The storm acts as a real and symbolic threat, heightening the sense of vulnerability.

title: The Three Stooges
justification: Perceived threat is a recurring theme, though not dominant. The nuns express fear of the boys, with Sister Ricardo avoiding them due to her "nerves." Sister Mary-Mengele is portrayed as a disciplinarian, suggesting a need to control the boys' disruptive behavior. The boys themselves face the threat of foster care, which Peezer explicitly fears due to his brother's experience: "Forget it! I'm not going to end up like Peezer's brother, Weezer." Moe's initial reluctance to be adopted stems from a fear of separation from his friends, highlighting vulnerability.

title: Here Comes the Boom
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of perceived threat as a central theme. While characters face challenges like budget cuts and job insecurity, these are presented more as obstacles to overcome than as pervasive threats. There are isolated moments of vulnerability, such as the principal's potential firing, but these are not driven by a sense of constant danger or paranoia. The dialogue focuses more on community, support, and problem-solving than on fear or distrust of the outside world. The narrative emphasizes resilience and collective action, suggesting a generally safe environment where challenges can be addressed through cooperation.

title: Red Dawn
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film, with the characters facing constant danger from an invading force. The dialogue emphasizes the loss of control and the need for survival, such as when Robert says, "...no longer controlled by the government of the United States. Don't go outside unless it's an absolute emergency." Jed's military background is used to highlight the severity of the situation, as he explains, "When I was overseas, we were the good guys. We enforced order. Now we're the bad guys and we create chaos." The film's narrative is driven by the characters' fear of the occupying forces and their determination to fight back, despite being outgunned and outnumbered, as Jed states, "We inherited our freedom. Now it's up to all of us to fight for it."

title: Resident Evil: Retribution
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the provided subtitles. The dialogue establishes a world overrun by viral outbreaks and mutated creatures, where survival is a constant struggle. Alice and other characters are relentlessly pursued by the Umbrella Corporation and its agents, as evidenced by lines like "Shoot to kill" and "They're headed this way. Her orders are to recapture you... terminate you if necessary." The Red Queen's control over the facility and her attempts to kill Alice and her allies further emphasize the pervasive danger. The constant need for escape, the presence of bioweapons, and the threat of betrayal all contribute to a high level of perceived threat.

title: The Cabin in the Woods
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme, with characters constantly facing danger and making decisions based on fear. The dialogue emphasizes the characters' vulnerability to external forces, both natural and supernatural. The characters are manipulated and terrorized by unseen forces, creating a pervasive atmosphere of danger. The dialogue highlights the idea that the world is not safe and that there are powerful entities that seek to harm humanity, as evidenced by the constant references to the "ancient ones" and the need to appease them.

title: What to Expect When You’re Expecting
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of perceived threat. Characters face personal challenges like career setbacks and relationship issues, but these are not presented as pervasive threats from the outside world. There are isolated moments of stress, such as Wendy's anxiety about her pregnancy and career, and Alex's initial fear of fatherhood, but these are largely internal and resolved through personal growth and support from their communities. The narrative focuses more on the joys and challenges of parenthood and relationships than on external dangers or a sense of pervasive vulnerability.

title: End of Watch
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film, driven by the officers' constant exposure to violence, gang activity, and the inherent dangers of their profession. The dialogue is replete with examples of this: the opening monologue of the police officer emphasizes the potential for violence ('If you shoot at me, I will shoot back'), and the subsequent scenes depict high-speed chases, violent confrontations ('Fuck you!'), and the ever-present threat of gang warfare ('Curbside Gang's at it again, bro.'). The officers themselves acknowledge the danger ('Watch the street. Make sure no assholes come up here and kill us.'). The discovery of tortured bodies further amplifies the sense of a dangerous world, and the warning from Tre about a 'hit' on the officers reinforces the constant threat they face.

title: The Artist
justification: The subtitles contain some elements of perceived threat, but it is not a dominant theme. George Valentin faces the threat of obsolescence in the face of changing industry trends, expressed through lines like "People want new faces, talking faces" and "Out with the old, in with the new." He also faces financial ruin, indicated by "It looks like we've gone bust" and the auction of his possessions. However, these threats are more circumstantial than pervasive, and the narrative does not consistently emphasize fear or paranoia. The dialogue also includes instances of violence, such as "Get Back here,you loser!", but these are isolated.

title: This is 40
justification: While the subtitles contain instances of conflict and negative emotions, a pervasive sense of threat is not structurally central. Characters experience interpersonal conflicts, financial worries, and anxieties about aging, but these are not presented as existential threats. For example, Debbie and Pete argue about finances and infidelity, but their relationship issues don't create a sense of constant danger. Sadie's online interactions and the confrontation with Joseph's mother introduce some threat, but these are isolated incidents. The overall tone is more comedic and domestic than suspenseful or paranoid.

title: Rock of Ages
justification: The film presents a moderate level of perceived threat. While not the central driving force, vulnerability and danger are recurring elements. Early in the film, Sherrie is mugged upon arrival in Hollywood, highlighting the immediate dangers of the setting: "Give me that! Let go! Come on! Let me have it! No! No!" Later, Patricia Whitmore's "Clean Up The Strip" initiative aims to eliminate what she perceives as a threat to the city's youth, framing rock 'n' roll as a "disease." Dennis Dupree also expresses concern about the club's future, fearing its potential closure due to financial troubles and external pressures.

title: Abraham Lincoln: Vampire Hunter
justification: The film establishes a world where vampires are a constant, hidden threat, driving the protagonist's actions and shaping his relationships. Dialogue such as Henry's warning, "Anyone in this well-mannered city might very well be one of them," creates a pervasive sense of paranoia and distrust. Abraham's training and subsequent vampire hunting are motivated by the threat they pose to his loved ones and the nation, as highlighted by Henry's statement, "It falls to us, Abraham, the hunters, to keep the balance. To ensure that this remains a nation of men, and not monsters." The narrative emphasizes the need for vigilance and the ever-present danger lurking beneath the surface of everyday life, making perceived threat a central theme.

title: Lawless
justification: The narrative is steeped in a sense of threat stemming from the illegal moonshining business and the violent world it inhabits. Dialogue such as, "It'll come at you like a knife, pointy end first, sharp and hot all the way down," illustrates the ever-present danger associated with their product. The arrival of Special Deputy Rakes from Chicago escalates the threat, as he aims to control the county through intimidation and violence, highlighted by his statement, "I'm the one who's going to make your life real difficult from now on." The Bondurant brothers face constant threats from rival gangs, corrupt law enforcement, and the ever-present possibility of betrayal, as Jimmy says, "For things to run smooth, you got to grease the tracks." The pervasive atmosphere of danger and the need for vigilance are central to the plot, driving the characters' decisions and actions.

title: That’s My Boy
justification: While the film contains instances of characters facing immediate threats (e.g., legal trouble, physical altercations), a pervasive sense of environmental threat is not structurally central. Donny faces legal consequences for tax evasion, indicated by the line, "Well, they said a lot of stuff. The thing that really jumped out was 'three years in prison.'" There are also moments of physical threat, such as when Chad threatens Todd, stating, "if you ever do anything to hurt my sister, I will take my government-issued service revolver, stick it straight up your fuppin' poop chute, and empty the clip." However, these threats are localized and do not create a sustained atmosphere of paranoia or widespread danger. The characters generally navigate their world without constant fear, suggesting that perceived threat is intermittent rather than a dominant structural element.

title: Trouble with the Curve
justification: The subtitles contain a minimal sense of pervasive threat. Characters occasionally express concern for each other's well-being, such as Pete's worry about Gus's health and job security ("Mick, if something goes wrong up in Carolina with this kid Gentry...he's gonna be out of a job."). There's also a brief moment of physical threat when Mickey is harassed at a bar, leading to a confrontation ("You ever touch her again, I'm gonna rip your fucking face off."). However, these instances are isolated and do not establish a consistent atmosphere of danger or vulnerability. The narrative primarily focuses on baseball scouting and personal relationships, rather than a world where characters are constantly at risk.

title: Step Up Revolution
justification: The subtitles present a world where characters face potential threats from various sources, contributing to a moderate sense of perceived threat. There are explicit mentions of the possibility of going to jail ("I say 50% chance to get to jail tonight.") and the need to fight for what one wants ("And there comes a time when you have to shout, fight for what you want."). The characters also face the threat of losing their homes and community due to real estate development ("Buying the coast on this side of the river. This is a bar, a house, a shop, where your sister is working... All is lost."). While not pervasive, these elements create a recurring sense of danger and the need for vigilance, especially concerning the characters' livelihoods and freedom.

title: Tyler Perry's Good Deeds
justification: The film's subtitles reveal a recurring sense of threat and vulnerability, though it's not the dominant structural element. Lindsey's homelessness and fear of losing her daughter to Child Welfare create a constant state of anxiety, exemplified by her hiding Ariel in a closet and her desperation to find stable housing. The dialogue also highlights the dangers of the outside world, such as Wesley mentioning his secretary getting mugged and Denise warning Lindsey to keep her belongings close at the shelter. Walter's erratic behavior and the family's business troubles contribute to an atmosphere of instability and potential harm, though these threats are often interpersonal rather than environmental.

title: Frankenweenie
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the narrative. The townspeople exhibit fear and distrust towards Victor and his science, fueled by unusual events and Mr. Rzykruski's eccentric behavior. Dialogue such as, "I just don't feel safe walking by there," and "Sometimes I wonder just what goes on in that house," illustrates the community's growing unease and suspicion. This fear escalates when the reanimated creatures wreak havoc, leading the townspeople to hunt Sparky and Victor, shouting, "Kill the monster!" and "Where's my niece? He's killed the little girl!" The narrative emphasizes the danger and paranoia that arise from misunderstanding and fear of the unknown.

title: The Watch
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme. The narrative quickly establishes a sense of danger with the murder of Antonio, described as being "ripped apart by a wild animal." This event sparks fear and paranoia, leading to the formation of the neighborhood watch. The threat escalates with the discovery of aliens, who are described as skin-stealing invaders. Dialogue such as "We are already among you" and the revelation that "They're among us" reinforces the idea that anyone could be a threat, driving the characters' actions and decisions.

title: Parental Guidance
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of perceived threat. While there are moments of family tension and personal anxieties (Artie's job loss, Harper's audition pressure, Barker's imaginary friend), these do not translate into a broader sense of pervasive danger or vulnerability. The dialogue focuses on family dynamics, career aspirations, and personal growth, rather than fear or paranoia. The closest example would be Diane's comment about impending doom when it starts raining, but this is quickly dismissed as a joke.

title: 2016: Obama’s America
justification: The documentary subtitles contain recurring references to potential threats, both domestic and international, contributing to a moderate sense of unease. The film highlights concerns about America's vulnerability due to Obama's policies, such as slashing the nuclear arsenal and taking a perceived anti-Israel stance: "leaving America vulnerable." There is also a sense of threat from radical Islam and the potential for a more dangerous world if America's influence diminishes: "It will be a much more vicious environment in which wars will be more common." The film also suggests that Obama's policies are designed to weaken America and redistribute wealth globally, which could be interpreted as a threat to the American way of life.

title: House at the End of the Street
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film, driven by the history of a double murder and the lingering presence of the alleged perpetrator's sister. Dialogue frequently references the murders, creating an atmosphere of unease and suspicion. Characters express fear and distrust of Ryan Jacobson, the son of the murdered couple, and rumors circulate about Carrie Anne, the sister, living in the woods. Sarah's overprotectiveness of Elissa, stemming from a fear of the dangers in their new environment, further emphasizes the theme. The climax involves Ryan's descent into madness, fueled by his obsession with Carrie Anne, culminating in a violent confrontation that underscores the ever-present threat.

title: Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the film, driven by the aftermath of 9/11 and its impact on Oskar's sense of safety and the world around him. The dialogue reveals Oskar's anxieties and fears, such as his statement, "Bridges make me especially panicky," and his detailed list of things that make him panicky, including "airplanes...tall things...things you can get stuck in." The film also highlights the mother's constant worry for Oskar's safety, as she admits, "Every hour of every day. I couldn't breathe until the door closed," revealing a pervasive fear of harm befalling her son. The Renter's character, initially presented as potentially dangerous ("Is he dangerous? If you ever see him, don't say anything. He can get very angry."), further contributes to the atmosphere of threat and uncertainty.

title: Iron Man 3
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the narrative. Tony Stark's home is attacked after he threatens the Mandarin, forcing him to flee and protect Pepper Potts. The Mandarin's terrorist acts create a pervasive sense of fear and vulnerability, as seen in the news reports and public reactions: "The nation remains on high alert." The narrative emphasizes the constant danger and the need for vigilance, with characters like Happy Hogan expressing concern for Pepper's safety and the world getting "weird." The film also explores the idea of creating one's own demons, suggesting that fear and paranoia can be self-fulfilling prophecies.

title: The Hunger Games: Catching Fire
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this narrative, driven by the oppressive control of the Capitol and the constant fear of rebellion. President Snow's explicit threats to Katniss, such as, "You should imagine thousands upon thousands of your people dead. This town of yours reduced to ashes," establish a high level of danger. The Victory Tour becomes a performance under duress, with Katniss forced to maintain a facade of love to prevent further repercussions. The escalation of violence in the districts, described by Gale as, "There were people fighting in the streets, and fires, and Peacekeepers were gunning them down," reinforces the pervasive sense of threat and vulnerability. The Quarter Quell adds another layer of danger, as the Victors are forced to fight again, highlighting the Capitol's arbitrary power and the characters' lack of control over their lives.

title: Despicable Me 2
justification: The subtitles contain some elements of perceived threat, but they are not structurally central. Gru is recruited by the Anti-Villain League because a dangerous serum, PX-41, has been stolen, and they believe a master criminal is behind it. This sets up a plot where danger is present, but it is not pervasive. Gru's past as a villain and the existence of powerful villains like El Macho contribute to a sense of potential threat, as does the transformation serum. However, much of the dialogue focuses on humor, family dynamics, and romantic interests, which dilutes the overall sense of threat.

title: Man of Steel
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the film, driven by the impending destruction of Krypton and the subsequent threat posed by General Zod. The dialogue emphasizes the urgency and danger of Krypton's collapse, with characters stating, "Krypton's core is collapsing" and "We may only have a matter of weeks." Zod's arrival on Earth and his ultimatum, "Surrender within 24 hours...or watch this world suffer the consequences," establishes a clear and immediate threat to humanity. The film also explores the fear and distrust of the unknown, as people react with fear and suspicion towards Superman, highlighting a 'Mean World Syndrome' where strangers are seen as dangerous.

title: Monsters University
justification: The subtitles contain some elements of perceived threat, but it is not a dominant theme. There are warnings about the 'dangerous area' of the Scare Floor and the 'extremely toxic' nature of human children, suggesting a potential for harm. Characters are told to 'stay close together' and 'don't cross over that safety line.' However, these threats are largely presented as manageable risks within a controlled environment, and the overall tone is more adventurous and comedic than genuinely fearful. The Scare Games are described as 'crazy dangerous' where 'you could totally die,' but this is framed as an exciting challenge rather than a source of pervasive anxiety.

title: Frozen
justification: The theme of perceived threat is moderately salient in "Frozen." The narrative establishes a world where Elsa's powers are both beautiful and dangerous, leading to her isolation and the locking of the kingdom's gates. Dialogue such as "Fear will be your enemy" and the constant need to "Conceal it. Don't feel it. Don't let it show" highlight the pervasive fear surrounding Elsa's abilities. The Duke of Weselton's paranoia about Elsa's powers further contributes to the sense of threat, as he declares, "There's sorcery in you," and insists, "She must be stopped!" While the film ultimately resolves with love and acceptance, the initial and recurring emphasis on the dangers of Elsa's powers and the fear they inspire creates a significant sense of perceived threat.

title: Gravity
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the film, as evidenced by the constant danger the characters face from the debris field. The dialogue emphasizes the urgency and the high stakes of the situation, such as when Houston declares, "Mission abort. Repeat, mission abort. Initiate emergency disconnect from Hubble. Begin reentry procedure." The characters are in constant fear of the next impact, and their decisions are driven by the need to survive. The loss of communication with Earth further amplifies the sense of isolation and vulnerability, as seen in Stone's repeated calls: "Houston, do you copy?" The narrative is structured around the characters' struggle against a hostile environment, making perceived threat a dominant force.

title: Fast and Furious 6
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film, as characters constantly face danger from external forces. The dialogue emphasizes the high stakes and potential for betrayal, such as when Hobbs recruits Dom's team, stating, "If you want to catch wolves, you need wolves." The threat posed by Owen Shaw and his crew is consistently highlighted, with Hobbs describing them as "world-class" and capable of causing "unthinkable" loss of life. Dom's team is also targeted, with Shaw threatening to "break you whenever I want." The film's narrative is driven by the need to protect family and prevent catastrophic events, underscoring the pervasive sense of threat.

title: Oz the Great and Powerful
justification: The narrative contains a recurring sense of danger and the need for vigilance, particularly concerning the Wicked Witch and her minions. Characters frequently express fear and vulnerability, such as the townspeople's terror of the Wicked Witch's attacks ("Last night, the whole town was celebrating... But then those things flew in.") and the China Girl's fear of being captured. The Wicked Witch herself poses a significant threat, poisoning her own father and attempting to destroy the land. The dialogue emphasizes the constant threat of attack and the need for protection, contributing to a pervasive atmosphere of danger, but it is not the dominant structural engine.

title: Star Trek Into Darkness
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film, with characters constantly facing danger and making decisions based on fear. The initial volcano mission highlights the risk of violating the Prime Directive and the potential for planetary destruction. The threat escalates with John Harrison's attacks on Starfleet, leading to a manhunt and the looming possibility of war with the Klingons. Admiral Marcus's manipulation and militaristic agenda further amplify the sense of danger and distrust. The film culminates in a desperate battle to save Earth, with characters facing death and destruction at every turn, solidifying the structural importance of perceived threat.

title: Thor: The Dark World
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film. The narrative revolves around the Dark Elves' desire to plunge the universe into eternal darkness using the Aether, an ancient weapon of immense destructive power. Dialogue such as "Their deaths will mean our survival" and "I will reclaim the Aether. I will restore our world. And I will put an end to this poisoned universe" highlights the constant threat of annihilation. Characters are frequently in danger, and the film emphasizes the need for vigilance and sacrifice to protect Asgard and the Nine Realms, as seen in Odin's and Thor's discussions about the impending war and the potential loss of life.

title: World War Z
justification: Perceived threat is a dominant structural engine in this narrative. The film opens with news reports of global outbreaks, environmental disasters, and strange behaviors, immediately establishing a world on the brink. Dialogue such as "Authorities have confirmed an avian flu outbreak," "Police say they've seen similar cases recently of people behaving strangely," and "The government has declared martial law" creates a pervasive sense of impending doom. As the zombie outbreak escalates, characters constantly face immediate threats to their safety, exemplified by lines like "Get back in your car right now!" and "We've got to get out of the city." The narrative is driven by the characters' desperate attempts to survive in a world overrun by zombies, making perceived threat the central engine of the plot.

title: The Hobbit: The Desolation of Smaug
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this narrative. Characters frequently express fear and vulnerability, and the dialogue emphasizes the dangers lurking in the world. Gandalf warns of 'darker minds' turning towards Erebor and the growing threat of Orcs. Beorn's unpredictable nature and the dangers of Mirkwood are highlighted, with warnings about getting lost and being hunted. The presence of Azog and the Necromancer, along with the threat of dragon fire, creates a pervasive atmosphere of danger and paranoia, driving the characters' decisions and actions.

title: The Croods
justification: The theme of perceived threat is central to the narrative. The Croods' lives are governed by Grug's strict rules, which are rooted in fear of the outside world. Dialogue such as "Anything new is bad, curiosity is bad. Going out at night is bad. Basically, anything fun is bad," and "Darkness brings death. We know this," highlights the constant sense of danger. The family's survival depends on adhering to these rules, emphasizing their vulnerability to the environment. The narrative arc revolves around the Croods' journey to a safer place, driven by the threat of the world ending, further solidifying the theme's structural importance.

title: The Heat
justification: The film's narrative is significantly driven by a sense of threat and vulnerability, though not to a pervasive degree. Characters frequently encounter dangerous situations, and there's a recurring emphasis on the need for vigilance. For example, Ashburn's investigation into Larkin involves navigating a criminal underworld where violence and betrayal are commonplace, as evidenced by the dialogue: "If I tell you, that's my ass chopped up into a million motherfucking pieces!" and "They're maniacs. They'll chop you up, or gun you down, or worse." Mullins's familiarity with the streets stems from the constant threat of violence and crime, and her family is directly targeted by Larkin, forcing them into hiding. The pervasive sense of danger is further highlighted by the constant presence of weapons and the characters' readiness to use them.

title: We’re the Millers
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in "We're the Millers." The narrative is driven by David's initial vulnerability to Brad, a dangerous drug dealer, after being robbed: "If you take that my boss will kill me." This leads to the high-stakes smuggling operation, where the threat of violence and imprisonment looms large: "If I try to cross the border with more than a pound, you're talking like, um... Twenty-five years in Mexican prison." The family's encounters with Pablo Chacon and the corrupt cop further emphasize the constant danger, with threats of death and sexual assault: "You all die now." The film relies on the characters' vulnerability and the potential for harm to drive the plot and create tension.

title: The Great Gatsby
justification: While not a dominant theme, perceived threat appears intermittently throughout the narrative. There are instances of characters expressing cynicism and a sense of unease about the world, such as Daisy's statement, "I think everything's terrible anyhow. I've been everywhere and seen everything and done everything. I've had a very bad time...I'm pretty cynical about everything." Tom's racist remarks and assertion that "Civilization's going to pieces" also contribute to a sense of societal decay and potential danger. The Valley of Ashes is described as a "grotesque place," and the eyes of Doctor T.J. Eckleburg "brooded over it all," creating a feeling of being watched and judged. These elements suggest a world where characters are not entirely safe or trusting, but it is not a pervasive or central theme.

title: The Conjuring
justification: The subtitles depict a family terrorized by a demonic presence, creating a pervasive sense of threat. Dialogue such as "It scares us just thinking about it," and "We are beyond terrified. We don't know what's going on or what to do," establishes a high level of fear and vulnerability. The Warrens' warnings, like "It's safer for these things to be in here than out there," and Lorraine's visions of a "dark entity" latched onto the family, reinforce the idea of a constant, lurking danger. The narrative revolves around the family's struggle against this threat, driving their decisions and actions, and making perceived threat a central structural element.

title: Identity Thief
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film, driven by identity theft and its consequences. Sandy Patterson's life is upended when his identity is stolen, leading to financial ruin, legal troubles, and professional jeopardy. The dialogue highlights his growing fear and vulnerability as he faces arrest warrants, credit card fraud, and accusations of drug dealing. Cornish threatens Sandy after he quits, saying "I'm coming for you. And I'm killing you everywhere." The narrative emphasizes the constant danger and need for vigilance as Sandy attempts to clear his name and reclaim his life, culminating in a cross-country pursuit of the identity thief.

title: Grown Ups 2
justification: Perceived threat is a recurring theme, though not dominant. There are multiple instances of characters expressing fear for their safety or the safety of their children. For example, Adam Sandler's character says, "My God, riding their bikes to school. Couldn't do that in L.A. with the nuts out there." Later, he expresses concern about his son playing football, saying, "Avoid big idiots trying to hurt you." The film also includes a scene where the main characters are confronted by hostile college students, leading to a fight, and another where a character is stalked by a former bully, creating a sense of unease and potential danger.

title: The Wolverine
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film. The narrative is saturated with danger, from the initial bombing sequence to the Yakuza's pursuit of Mariko. Logan is constantly fighting off attackers, and characters repeatedly emphasize the danger they are in. Dialogue such as "It's not safe," "They're going to kill her," and "There have been attacks. Attempted kidnappings. Attempted assassinations" highlights the pervasive sense of threat. The film's plot is driven by the need to protect Mariko from various forces seeking to harm or control her, making perceived threat a key structural element.

title: G.I. Joe: Retaliation
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film. The narrative begins with a high-stakes mission to extract a defector, emphasizing the constant need for vigilance and readiness for combat. The dialogue frequently mentions enemies, insurgents, and potential attacks, creating a sense of danger lurking just outside the characters' safe zones. The assassination of the Pakistani president and the subsequent threat of nuclear war further amplify the feeling of a dangerous world. The Joes are framed as vulnerable to betrayal, as evidenced by the attack on their base and the revelation of an imposter President, driving major decisions and actions throughout the film.

title: Now You See Me
justification: The film subtitles contain a recurring sense of threat, though it is not the dominant structural element. Characters are frequently in situations where they are vulnerable to harm, betrayal, or crime, such as when the magician's assistant is told to close the door because it's a "bad apartment building." The dialogue also emphasizes the potential for deception and manipulation, as seen in the opening monologue about how easily people can be fooled. The characters are often pursued by law enforcement or other antagonists, creating a sense of danger and the need for vigilance, as when the FBI chases the Four Horsemen after their performances.

title: Cloudy with a Chance of Meatballs 2
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film. The narrative establishes a world where food has become monstrous and dangerous, requiring constant vigilance and action to prevent widespread destruction. Flint's initial invention, the FLDSMDFR, is framed as a source of potential global catastrophe, with dialogue emphasizing the need to destroy it to prevent the food monsters from reaching the mainland and destroying monuments like Lady Liberty. Chester V's manipulation of Flint is predicated on the idea of an imminent threat from the food creatures, driving Flint's decisions and actions. The film also includes scenes of characters being attacked by food creatures, reinforcing the idea that the environment is inherently dangerous.

title: Lee Daniels' The Butler
justification: The provided subtitles consist solely of error messages related to server access. There is no dialogue or narrative content present. Therefore, it is impossible to assess the salience of perceived threat within the narrative, as there is no narrative to analyze. The absence of any character interaction or plot elements means there is no basis for evaluating fear, vulnerability, or environmental danger.

title: The Hangover 3
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme, driven by the characters' entanglement with dangerous criminals. The narrative is propelled by the threat posed by Marshall, who kidnaps Doug and threatens to kill him if the group doesn't deliver Chow. This is evident in dialogue such as, "You don't give me Chow, I blow his brains out." and "You go to the cops...I blow his brains out." The characters are constantly in fear of Marshall's violence, and the narrative emphasizes their vulnerability to his power. The pervasive sense of danger is further heightened by Chow's unpredictable and violent behavior, as well as the constant threat of being caught by the authorities.

title: Epic
justification: The narrative is significantly driven by a sense of pervasive threat. The Boggans represent a constant and active danger to the forest and its inhabitants, as evidenced by their repeated border crossings and the ambush that leads to Queen Tara's death. Characters frequently express fear and concern about the Boggans' actions, such as Ronin's warnings about their aggression and the general panic following the queen's demise. The dialogue emphasizes the vulnerability of the forest and its inhabitants, with the Boggans actively seeking to destroy the balance of nature and plunge the world into darkness. The need to protect the Royal Pod and ensure the continuation of life further underscores the central role of perceived threat in the narrative.

title: Captain Phillips
justification: The film's narrative is heavily driven by the constant threat of piracy and violence. Dialogue such as "We are going around the Horn of Africa, right?" and "We got pirate cages. They were all open. All the doors are unlocked. I want everything closed, locked, even in port" establishes the ever-present danger. The crew's repeated drills and the captain's heightened security measures, like "Tighten up security," underscore the perceived threat. The pirates' violent actions and threats, such as "Every crew, one minute, I will kill someone," and the crew's fear, exemplified by "I'm telling you now that they're not paying me enough to fight pirates," further emphasize the salience of perceived threat. The film structurally relies on this threat to create tension and drive the plot.

title: Silver Linings Playbook
justification: The subtitles contain a moderate level of perceived threat. Pat's mental instability and past violent actions create a sense of unease, as evidenced by Officer Keogh's frequent visits and the neighbors' fear ("People are scared. I gotta come in."). The restraining order against Pat highlights a tangible threat to Nikki. Additionally, Ronnie's anxieties and reliance on Veronica's control suggest a vulnerability to external pressures. While not pervasive, these elements contribute to a recurring theme of potential danger and instability.

title: Pacific Rim
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this narrative. The film establishes a world under constant threat from Kaiju attacks, leading to widespread fear and the need for constant vigilance. Dialogue such as "When alien life entered our world it was from deep beneath the Pacific Ocean," and "This was not gonna stop. This was just the beginning," immediately sets a tone of impending doom. Characters frequently discuss the escalating danger, with lines like, "The Kaiju are learning our defenses. They're adapting. Evolving. And we're losing Jaegers faster than we can build them," highlighting the growing vulnerability of humanity. The narrative emphasizes the need for extreme measures, such as the Jaeger program, to combat this pervasive threat, further solidifying its structural importance.

title: This is the End
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the narrative. The initial threat emerges with the 'earthquake' and escalates as characters are sucked into the sky. This event is followed by reports of looting, rioting, and martial law, creating a sense of societal breakdown. Characters express fear and paranoia, boarding up the house and arming themselves. The narrative emphasizes the dangers outside, with characters facing threats from demons, cannibals, and the apocalypse, driving their decisions and actions.

title: Jackass Presents: Bad Grandpa
justification: The film's subtitles suggest a world where characters are frequently exposed to danger, betrayal, and exploitation, although this is often played for comedic effect. The opening scene involves a child discussing his mother's drug addiction and arrest, highlighting vulnerability. The main character, Irving, encounters numerous bizarre and potentially threatening situations, including a man with his penis stuck in a soda machine and various encounters with eccentric and potentially dangerous individuals. The dialogue also includes instances of theft, drug use, and general social dysfunction, contributing to a sense of underlying threat and instability.

title: Olympus Has Fallen
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film, with the White House under constant attack and the President's life in danger. The dialogue emphasizes the vulnerability of the President and his staff, as well as the constant need for vigilance. For example, the phrase "Code 999" is repeated, indicating a state of emergency. The dialogue also highlights the potential for betrayal, as seen with Forbes's actions. The film's narrative is driven by the threat of nuclear war and the constant danger lurking within the White House.

Perceived threat is a central theme in the narrative, driven by the pervasive racism and hostility Jackie Robinson faces. Dialogue such as "Get out, nigger!" and "We don't want you here!" demonstrates the constant verbal abuse and threats of violence. The film highlights Robinson's vulnerability through scenes where he is denied service, threatened with physical harm, and targeted with racial slurs, creating a palpable sense of danger. Mr. Rickey explicitly warns Robinson about the vitriol he will face, emphasizing the need to control his temper to avoid validating racist stereotypes, further solidifying the theme of threat and vulnerability.

title: Zero Dark Thirty
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the film, driven by the constant fear of terrorist attacks and the vulnerability of both civilians and intelligence personnel. The dialogue frequently mentions potential targets like consulates and Marriotts, highlighting the ever-present danger. Characters express fear of being targeted, as seen when one character is warned, "Any American in Pakistan is a target." The film also emphasizes the difficulty in identifying and preventing attacks, contributing to a pervasive sense of unease and the need for constant vigilance. The interrogation scenes, with threats of violence and torture, further amplify the sense of danger and vulnerability.

title: Elysium
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the film, with characters constantly facing danger and vulnerability. Max's parole officer warns him about his high chance of regressing to old behavior patterns, highlighting the ever-present threat of imprisonment. The dialogue emphasizes the zero-tolerance policy and the constant surveillance, creating an atmosphere of fear and control. The threat of violence is also evident, with characters like Kruger engaging in torture and other human rights violations. The film's narrative is driven by the characters' desire to escape the dangerous and oppressive environment of Earth and reach the safety and security of Elysium.

title: Anchorman 2: The Legend Continues
justification: While the film is largely comedic, there are intermittent moments where characters express a sense of vulnerability or threat. For example, Ron's son Walter expresses fear of a ghost in his closet, and Ron attempts to alleviate this fear, albeit clumsily. Later, Linda Jackson threatens Ron and his team after their broadcast, saying, "If you were a man, I'd knock you out." These moments, while not pervasive, contribute to a sense that the world is not entirely safe, though the overall tone remains lighthearted.

title: Disney Planes
justification: The subtitles contain some elements of perceived threat, but it is not a dominant theme. Characters express concern about the dangers of racing, such as turbine failure and wing flutter, and there are mentions of crashes and potential for harm. Dusty is warned about the risks of flying in certain weather conditions and at high altitudes. However, these threats are often presented as challenges to overcome rather than sources of pervasive fear. The dialogue also includes moments of camaraderie and support, which counteracts the sense of constant danger.

title: The Lone Ranger
justification: Perceived threat is a recurring theme in "The Lone Ranger," though not the dominant structural engine. The dialogue frequently alludes to the dangers of the Wild West, with characters expressing fear of outlaws and the Comanche. For example, characters repeatedly mention Butch Cavendish's brutality, such as eating a "Red-Legger's heart," creating an atmosphere of fear. The railroad executive, Cole, is presented as a manipulative figure who instigates conflict with the Comanche, heightening the sense of danger and vulnerability for settlers. Tonto's warnings about the "windigo" and the need for a "Spirit Walker" contribute to the pervasive sense of an environmental threat.

title: Oblivion
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in the film, as the characters live in a world where remnants of a scavenger army pose a constant danger. Jack and Vika's mission is to protect hydro rigs from these scavengers, who "attack our drones at night, and try to kill me during the day." The dialogue emphasizes the need for vigilance and the potential for sudden harm, as seen when Vika warns Jack to "be careful out there." The narrative also highlights the vulnerability of the characters, as they are constantly at risk of attack and betrayal, with the drones programmed to kill humans. The pervasive atmosphere of danger is further emphasized by the radiation zones and the unknown threats lurking in the outside world.

title: Insidious Chapter 2
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film, with characters constantly facing danger from supernatural entities. Dialogue such as "Something is following him," "There's something in this house. I can feel it. It doesn't want me here," and "I saw what haunts him, and it's not a friend. It's a parasite. I've never felt such a malignant presence. It wants to be him" establishes a pervasive sense of dread. The characters' fear drives their actions, including seeking help from paranormal experts and attempting to suppress a child's abilities to protect him from these threats. The narrative revolves around the family's vulnerability to these entities and their struggle to protect themselves, making perceived threat a dominant structural element.

title: Turbo
justification: While the film is largely optimistic, there are recurring moments of threat and vulnerability, particularly in the snails' natural environment. The constant threat of being 'smushed' in the tomato plant is a recurring motif, with characters frequently yelling 'Overripe!' as a warning. Chet's anxiety about the dangers of the outside world is also evident, as he warns Theo about 'shell crushers' and the need to 'tuck and roll.' The junkyard scene introduces a more explicit threat, with the snails facing potential harm from Whiplash and his crew, who talk about 'dead meat' and a 'slaughter.' These elements contribute to a sense of danger, but it is not a dominant theme.

title: 2 Guns
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film, with characters constantly facing danger and betrayal. The dialogue is filled with references to violence, mistrust, and the need for self-preservation. For example, Little Toro is killed for skimming, and Stig and Bobby are double-crossed by multiple parties, including the CIA and the Navy. The constant threat of violence and betrayal drives the characters' actions and decisions, making perceived threat a structurally important element of the narrative. The line, "There is no code. You do whatever you gotta do, whatever it takes," encapsulates the pervasive sense of danger and the need for ruthless self-reliance.

title: White House Down
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film, as the narrative revolves around a violent takeover of the White House and the potential for widespread destruction. Dialogue such as "We're crashing the White House," "The White House is down," and "Shots fired. Code Black! Code Black!" establishes an immediate sense of danger. The constant threat of violence and betrayal is further emphasized by the presence of snipers, explosions, and the potential for nuclear war, as characters repeatedly state, "They're in the building," and "We need to exfilt...I got this!" The narrative is driven by the need to protect the President and prevent a catastrophic attack, making perceived threat a structurally significant element.

title: Mama
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme. The film opens with news of a murder-suicide, immediately establishing a dangerous world. The father's frantic escape with his daughters, marked by his aggressive driving and desperate attempts to evade capture, reinforces this threat. The girls' subsequent abandonment in the woods and the creation of an 'imaginary guardian' to protect them highlights their extreme vulnerability. Later, Annabel and Lucas face constant danger from 'Mama,' a supernatural entity, culminating in a climactic confrontation where the girls are at risk of being killed.

title: Safe Haven
justification: The narrative is significantly driven by a sense of threat, primarily stemming from Katie's past and the fear of her abusive husband finding her. This is evident in her initial paranoia and desire for isolation, as well as her reluctance to form connections. Dialogue such as "He's gonna find me. He's gonna find us" and "He doesn't quit" underscores the pervasive fear that dictates her actions. The arrival of her husband and the ensuing confrontation, which puts the lives of others at risk, confirms the validity and centrality of this perceived threat.

title: The Smurfs 2
justification: Perceived threat is a recurring theme, though not dominant. The film opens with the evil wizard Gargamel's diabolical plan to infiltrate and betray the Smurfs, immediately establishing a sense of danger. Smurfette's nightmares about her origins and belonging contribute to her vulnerability. Gargamel's pursuit of Smurf essence and his threats to the Smurfs' existence create a constant sense of danger, as exemplified by his plan to capture Smurfette and extract the secret formula. The Smurfs' need to rescue Smurfette from Gargamel's clutches drives much of the plot, highlighting their vulnerability and the external threat he poses.

title: The Best Man Holiday
justification: The subtitles contain minimal evidence of perceived threat. Characters face personal challenges like career setbacks and relationship issues, but these do not create a pervasive sense of danger or vulnerability to external threats. There are brief moments of conflict, such as Shelby's erratic behavior and the fight at the Christmas gathering, but these are isolated incidents that do not define the overall narrative. The dialogue focuses more on interpersonal relationships, personal growth, and reconciliation than on fear or paranoia. The most significant threat is Mia's illness, but this is presented as a medical issue rather than a societal one.

title: Percy Jackson: Sea of Monsters
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this film, as the narrative revolves around the vulnerability of half-bloods and the constant danger they face from monsters and Titans. The opening scene depicts Thalia's sacrifice to protect her friends, establishing the high stakes and the ever-present threat of death. The dialogue emphasizes the need for a protective barrier around Camp Half-Blood, highlighting the fear of external forces: "The barrier, to protect them from those who lived for their death." The prophecy about Percy's potential to destroy Olympus adds another layer of threat, creating a sense of impending doom and uncertainty. Characters are constantly battling monsters and dealing with betrayals, reinforcing the idea that the world is a dangerous place for half-bloods.

title: A Good Day to Die Hard
justification: The film's narrative is heavily structured around perceived threat, with characters constantly facing danger and betrayal. From the initial courtroom bombing to the numerous shootouts and chases, the protagonists are consistently in harm's way. Dialogue such as "Take Komarov alive... kill the other one" and "You're out of your depth, John" emphasizes the high stakes and the lethal consequences of failure. The pervasive sense of danger drives the characters' decisions, forcing them to constantly be on guard and adapt to rapidly changing threats, as seen when Jack says, "We need to keep on moving. We have to get this guy to a doctor."

title: Warm Bodies
justification: Perceived threat is a central theme in this narrative, driven by the constant danger posed by zombies and 'Boneys.' The dialogue emphasizes the need for vigilance and fear of the outside world, as characters like Julie are warned about the dangers beyond the wall: 'Corpses look human, they are not...they are beyond your help.'
